# Evaluation & Trade-offs

The recommendation experiment compared a naive single-LLM-call baseline with a stored deterministic reference across ten synthetic personas. Nine personas provide travel data covering the fixed twelve-month evaluation window, while one deliberately represents a newly onboarded customer with only a few days of history. Each Langfuse dataset item contains the raw `load_context` payload as input and the analysis engine's normalised per-category recommendations as expected output. The baseline derives its recommendations from the raw data in one model call. The reference arm returns the deterministic recommendations stored when the dataset was seeded. The experiment therefore evaluates subscription decisions, not the Advisor's conversational behaviour, tool selection, forecast quality, or modal-shift suggestions.

Both arms were scored with three deterministic validity checks named *plan-in-catalog*, *action-in-vocabulary*, and *savings-non-negative*, a deterministic comparison with the reference called *category-agreement*, and an LLM judge for numerical soundness named *recommendation-soundness*. Only the reference arm's perfect *category-agreement* follows by construction. In the three documented baseline runs, all three validity checks scored 1.00, while mean per-persona category agreement varied between 0.61 and 0.69. This indicates agreement with the deterministic reference in roughly two-thirds of the evaluated decisions, not independently verified correctness. The soundness judge passed none of the ten baseline items in each recorded run, while the reference scored 1.00. In Julia Berger's case, for example, the baseline selected both reference actions but estimated the annual saving from the BahnCard upgrade at €1,449.37 instead of the engine's €1,619.92.

## Historical Token Usage and Latency

A separate Langfuse measurement compared the synchronous `run_full_analysis` path with the baseline. This path includes the deterministic analysis and the two bounded LLM steps, but not the ReAct Advisor. In the recorded measurement, the main analysis used an average of 7,845 tokens compared with 46,619 for the baseline, a 5.9-fold difference. The difference reached 9.3-fold for input tokens because the baseline receives the complete leg-level history, while the main analysis passes aggregated information to its LLM steps. Input accounted for 69% of the baseline's tokens and was dominated by the raw trip history, whereas output accounted for 56% of the main analysis's tokens.

With one persona processed at a time, the synchronous analysis had a median end-to-end latency of 28.3 seconds compared with 71.1 seconds for the baseline. The recorded maximum was 64.6 seconds for the main analysis and 878.5 seconds for the baseline. These values measure total synchronous model work rather than the current dashboard response time, since the dashboard now returns the deterministic result before the slower enrichment runs in the background. Later reductions to the forecast prompt and concurrent execution of the two LLM steps were not measured again, so the figures are historical results rather than current performance guarantees. The underlying trade-off remains that deterministic calculations reduce model usage and improve reproducibility, but every new numerical capability must be implemented in code rather than added through a prompt.
